item.title: Is an ‘A.I. Agent’ Coming for Our Sourdough Starter?
item.description:
Before opening his eight Upside Pizza slice shops in New York City, Noam Grossman studied with the sourdough master Anthony Falco, and has faithfully kept his original starter alive and bubbling. Naturally leavened dough, he believes, holds the secret to Upside’s signature crisp-chewy crust.

But last week, in a basement near the Port Authority Bus Terminal, Mr. Grossman grew increasingly agitated as he realized the stuff he was about to pour into a Hobart mixer could upend all that.

Leaven, a laboratory-grown product, is a shelf-stable powder that eliminates the need for the live sourdough starter that has long been the pride and preoccupation of craft bakers.

“Now that I know what it does, it feels weird to hold in my hand,” Mr. Grossman said. “This is like an A.I. agent. It feels like an existential threat to thousands of years of tradition.”

Invented by two Colorado microbiologists who are also home bakers, Leaven arrived in stores in June. But it has been quietly adopted by some of the nation’s top bakers and pizza makers over the past two years.

When added to flour and water, the microbes in Leaven begin the work of fermentation, and can carry it outmore reliably than notoriously temperamental sourdough starters. It does not shorten or replace the fermentation process — the dough still has to rise and proof as usual — but it does jump-start it.

Still, many bakers I spoke to are leery of Leaven. In professional baking, prestige is often attached to the most time-consuming, challenging and traditional methods. The mystique of live sourdough starter is the basis of the craft baking movement that took hold in the United States in the 1970s and built national brands like Panera, La Brea and Izzio.

“The emotional connection is real,” said Chad Robertson, a pioneer of the movement who founded the Tartine bakeries and just opened Altbau in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. Serious bread bakers sometimes travel with their starter, exposing it to local strains of the wild yeasts that give sourdough breads their complex flavors. After nurturing his starter in Los Angeles for a decade, he took it to Australia, Germany, Mexico and Spain, while studying and teaching. “And then to Costa Rica for a month to surf,” he said.

Although doubtful about Leaven’s ability to replicate the effect of live starter, he was curious. “If it works,” he said. “It would be the holy grail.”

Only a few Leaven users agreed to speak about the product. Others declined, including some large companies that are testing it for use in fast-food sandwiches and supermarket breads. (Some industrial bakers around the world are already using similar products.)

Scarr Pimentel, the founder of Scarr’s, the high-profile Manhattan pizzeria that first became famous for using house-milled flour and natural leavening, confirmed that he uses Leaven in all his crusts, both on the Lower East Side and in Las Vegas, with no noticeable difference.

“It’s the ultimate hack,” said Christiano Wennmann, Scarr’s head baker, who said he had kept quiet for fear that every pizza maker would start using it. “I’ve been gatekeeping it, to be honest.”

Mr. Wennmann said Leaven’s consistent results make it irresistible for a business with multiple locations and employees. “It removes a variable from a very complicated process,” he said.

Leaven is the first consumer product to encapsulate not only strains of wild yeast, but also the beneficial bacteria that live in an active starter. It’s also gluten-free, unlike a flour-based starter.

Marc Magliozzi has been fixated on improving his pizza for the 16 years Dozzino in Hoboken, N.J., has been open. He started with commercial yeast, moved to a biga (an Italian sourdough method) and then to Leaven. He said it produces a less sour flavor than live starter, but preserves the chew and umami of long-fermented dough.

“I never really wanted pizza crust to be sour,” he said, citing the tang of the tomato sauce on top. “In 10 years I think the whole sourdough pizza thing will be over.”

Still the popularity of sourdough — which generally makes tastier, more substantial and more digestible breads — marches on. Three of Time magazine’s Best New Inventions of 2026 are sourdough-related: the Sourdough Sidekick, a countertop appliance from King Arthur Flour that automatically builds a starter; Dough Dissolve, an enzyme-based cleaning product; and Leaven. It is moving into sweet baking: Sweetgreen has just released a sourdough chocolate-chip cookie nationwide.

But the term “sourdough,” like “slow-fermented” and “naturally leavened,” isn’t regulated in any way. Anything can wear the label, from supermarket white bread with a dash of commercial sour flavoring to the $60 organic rye loaf from an Austrian baker that recently made a splashy debut in New York.

During the pandemic, many home cooks fell for the siren song of sourdough. But given the work of feeding, airing and measuring a starter — not to mention the constant pressure to use it up — many (including me) found that a starter can feel like yet another domestic burden.

Just like the packets of dry yeast that most home bakers use, Leaven can be kept in the pantry and used anytime. It still took me 14 hours of proofing, stretching and folding, but the focaccia I made with it tasted better — sweeter and wheatier — than the yeast-risen version I usually bake.

Leaven’s founders, the microbiologists Cameron Martino and James Gaffney, are also avid home brewers. In an interview, Mr. Martino said that dozens of brewer’s yeasts are available, each producing a distinct style, like ales, lagers and lambics. So, they wondered, why there was only one kind of baker’s yeast on the market?

Virtually all commercial dough in the United States is made with active dry yeast, the dehydrated, domesticated version of a single yeast strain that was isolated by the Fleischmann’s company in the 1930s. That strain was selected for its quick-rising qualities: It generates the most carbon dioxide in the least time, producing a puffy loaf with a soft crumb.

But, Mr. Martino said, “you lose flavors, textures and other alternatives when you push everything into gas.”

Long fermentation with certain microbes gives sourdoughs their characteristic taste and texture. When flour and water are exposed to air and mixed with water, the bacteria and yeasts in a starter (or in a pouch of Leaven) get to work, breaking down the flour’s carbohydrates into sugars that they can eat. The bacteria are beneficial lactobacilli, the same microbes that give dry-cured meats, aged cheeses and long-fermented kimchi their umami-rich flavor.

I found it difficult to wrap my mind around how wild yeasts and living bacteria can exist in a shelf-stable product. I put this question to Scott Wiener, a New York pizza expert who teaches classes and leads tours. “If you put a rhinoceros in a zoo, it’s still a rhinoceros, right?” he said.

I pushed back, pointing out that a rhinoceros in a zoo is still noticeably alive. Is this rhinoceros, perhaps, in an artificially induced coma? “Exactly,” he said.

Back in the basement at Upside Pizza, two days after Mr. Grossman mixed the dough, it was time to bake two identical pies: one with his starter and one with Leaven.

For a first outing, the Leaven crust came out quite well — soft and stretchy, charred well on the bottom and able to hold a New York fold. Asked if he thought he could create a perfect replica of his crust with Leaven, Mr. Grossman said yes.

And if he could, would he?

“Absolutely not,” he said. The starter he uses is more than 10 years old, and has been handed off from one pizzaiolo to another, all of them successful.

“It’s not going anywhere,” he said.

item.title: Why Nostalgia for Tamagotchis, the Needy Little Virtual Pets, Won’t Die
item.description:
Rachel Liew started collecting Tamagotchis in 2013, shortly after she graduated from college. Now 36, with a job in human resources, she owns more than 200 of the virtual pets.

“I love being able to be in a group of people who have the same interests as me,” said Liew, who lives in Singapore and considers herself part of the Tamagotchi’s global online fan community. “I can’t get that in real life.”

When Akihiro Yokoi had the idea for the toy in the mid-1990s, he didn’t know it would be a hit. Yokoi, who owned and operated the Japanese toy design studio Wiz Co., told The New York Times in 1997 that he had seen a commercial with a boy trying to take his pet turtle along on a trip. How nice it would be, Yokoi thought, if people had portable pets.

The pocket-size digital gadgets, which mimicked newborn baby chicks, required continuous care, feeding and attention and were among the first video games to be, initially, marketed primarily to girls. The Japanese edition of the Tamagotchi instruction manual was even made to resemble the health records mothers used to track their babies’ growth, Anne Allison wrote in “Millennial Monsters: Japanese Toys and the Global Imagination” (2006).

More than 100 million Tamagotchis have been sold since they first appeared in Japan in 1996 — more than 33 million of those in the United States, where they debuted a year later, the toy’s maker, Bandai Namco, said.

That number has continued to tick upward as the addictive egg-on-a-keychain has enjoyed a resurgence in popularity, particularly among millennial and Gen Z women. The TikTok creator Charli D’Amelio has been a global ambassador, and the KPop group BlackPink recently collaborated on a limited-edition version. (Around 40 percent of Tamagotchi owners are adults, according to a 2020 company survey.)

Julie Woodward, an organizer of the NYC Tamagotchi Club, said, “Something I hear quite often from people in New York City — who, like me, often live in very small apartments — is that they like nurturing virtual pets.” Woodward, 28, a content creator, added, “we get together and hang out and connect our devices.”

What is remarkable about the Tamagotchi is not only its cross-cultural appeal, but its longevity. While other virtual pets like Neopets and Webkinz have had comebacks, the Tamagotchi will not die. Last year its 38th model, the Tamagotchi Paradise, debuted, offering 51 characters across 12 species in nine languages and with Wi-Fi connectivity to friends’ devices and the online “Tamaverse.” (It still, though, requires two AAA batteries.)

Tamagotchis were available in dozens of North American countries by May 1997, as well as in Europe and parts of Asia. They proved so distracting that some schools banned them. Many mothers became de facto Tamagotchi moms, tasked with keeping their kids’ beloved pets alive while they were in class. (Tamagotchis die without proper care, but can be reset.)

The Tamagotchi would spend the next few years navigating the trend cycle and shifting consumer obsessions. By 1998, the virtual pets were already trying to fend off a fuzzy robot called the Furby — and sales were cooling from the staggering 70 million worldwide orders in 1997 alone.

But Bandai rolled out a new model, the Tamagotchi Connection, in 2004. It featured built-in infrared sensors that allowed owners to face off in mini-games, send messages, exchange gifts and even fall in love and get married.

“It’s driven by nostalgia, but when you add on today’s technology capabilities, I think they’ll actually end up being almost more fun today than they were 30 years ago,” said Peter Fader, a marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, who focuses on consumer behavior.

Luke Williams, 40, a graphic designer for the National Health Service in Birmingham, England, appreciates the analog gameplay.

“It helps me stay grounded and focused, not distracted by notifications popping up on my screen all day,” he said.

In recent years, a passionate online fan community has sprung up around the toys. Content creators on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube review new models, showcase massive collections, and share video tutorials on painting, bedazzling and creating custom shells.

More than 60 in-person clubs have also formed, with chapters in Chile, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines, Singapore and the United States.

“It’s a fun way to connect with people all over the world,” said Twoey Gray, 31, the founder of the Toronto Tamagotchi Club, which has attracted as many as 100 people to its in-person meet-ups.

Bandai Namco plans to mark the toy’s anniversary in New York City with a Times Square takeover on Sunday. A free pop-up party with photo booths, product demonstrations and giveaways will be capped by a half-hour evening takeover of digital billboards across Times Square.

Woodward, the NYC Tamagotchi Club host, is planning to go.

“I’m excited to see everyone having a real-life encounter with Tamagotchi, all at once,” she said. “That’s going to be such a cool experience.”

item.title: My A.I. Hack Emergency Plan
item.description:
The warnings are coming thick and fast: Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said that the Iranian government has its sights on U.S. energy, water and financial services systems.

Senior executives at A.I. companies say their tools could act on their own and wreak similar havoc — or human hackers could deploy A.I.

So imagine a nationwide power outage. Or consider a municipal water system that turns off or becomes unsafe. Maybe the internet stops working for a while, and a lot of important things that you are used to accessing on the fly — Waze for a teen driver to get home, Venmo to pay a caregiver — are suddenly unavailable.

There is no way to know the odds of any of this happening, but they are probably higher than they were a year ago. There is, as an Anthropic security executive put it recently, a “vulnerability tsunami” headed our way.

Some preparation seems prudent right about now.

Millions of people who are familiar with extreme weather already know the basic outlines of personal readiness. The rest of us probably don’t.

That included me and my underprepared family of four, in our midsize Brooklyn apartment building, until we made our own plans in recent weeks.

I am not a traditional “prepper,” and I didn’t exactly volunteer for this assignment. I’m a veteran personal finance columnist whose beat is beating the system. But editors know that when strange times necessitate resourcefulness — voting when you can’t get to the ballot box, chasing Covid vaccines when there’s a stampede for them, scoring scarce Bruce Springsteen tickets — I can help figure things out.

The federal government tells us all to be prepared to hunker down for three days as a general rule. It doesn’t take much more effort to be ready to fend for yourself for a week. And it stands to reason that if it has taken days to recover from weather-related blackouts or mistakes that result from minor telecommunications upgrades, it could take a week or more to solve problems that result from A.I.-enabled attacks.

So at least a week of readiness was my goal. Here’s what I planned and what I bought.

Also, rehearse. We intend to practice using everything we hadn’t owned before this month.

The people you love matter more than anything, so you’ll need a plan for where, how or if you’re going to meet up.

In the language of more traditional preppers, we hope to “bug in” and hunker down, not bug out and try to flee the city. A second home hours away with a month of firewood, a solar array and an ample natural spring is not our reality.

My wife also happens to be a colleague, so we’d make the seven-mile trek home together as efficiently as possible and collect our 11 year-old from school along the way.

Our other daughter is at college much of the year. If we’re unable to communicate, the plan is for her to stay in her apartment there, with friends, relying at first on whatever food the school could provide.

Although she’s within reasonable driving distance, she has no car, and the roads between here and there are already prone to gridlock. She would make her own call about whether to try to travel back to us after a few days, and only in a group for safety.

I’m also making her take the Rand McNally Road Atlas I got her for her 16th birthday back to school after Thanksgiving. Paper maps are scarce these days, but they shouldn’t be.

For at least the first few hours after a power outage, many stores would try to stay open temporarily. If electronic payments are impossible, having at least $500 in cash on hand in small bills would be useful. Build up to it over months if you need to, $20 bill by bill.

There may be outages that affect only the banking system and not the energy grid. If A.T.M.s or credit card terminals don’t work for a while — or your individual bank’s or region’s machinery is not functioning — you could need a fair bit of real money. Some Chase A.T.M.s were indeed not working when the bank had technical difficulties earlier this week.

The body needs more water, sooner, than it does food, so provisioning ought to start here in preparation for many types of outages. At the first sign of trouble, fill any bathtubs, sinks and containers.

A World Health Organization guide suggests a gallon of water per day, per person for consumption. Our plan: No bathing (though we usually have packages of baby wipes around), no cooking (unless we still have gas), no dishes, minimal flushing.

We chose to buy drinking water to have on hand just in case, which necessitates shelf Jenga and purges in our storage-constrained apartment.

If you rely on municipal water, you may want to purify it if you’re worried that it is unsafe. We’ve bought supplies for that, and my colleagues at Wirecutter offer advice on containers, water treatment and all manner of other emergency supplies.

Those of you with electricity-powered wells will need a backup plan for power or manual pumping.

A guide from W.H.O. and other agencies suggests 2,100 calories per person per day to meet basic survival needs. There are plenty of ways to achieve that for a week with a limited selection of nutrient-dense, shelf-stable food. We’ve got a supply of peanut butter, canned chicken, fruit purée packets, cooked chickpeas and ready-to-eat lentils — and a manual can opener.

You won’t be alone in those aisles of the store. This week, Costco’s chief financial officer told Bloomberg that the retailer has recorded higher sales of rice, water and generators in recent weeks.

If you have large solar panels on your house, power may not be a concern. Other homeowners install whole-house generators or have portable ones. None of that works for most apartment dwellers, including me.

The search for a power solution should begin with the problem, like whether an outage could disable medical equipment. Our family is lucky; we don’t need to keep life-sustaining gear running or take temperature-sensitive prescription drugs.

One concern for us is losing our electric heat. Portable power stations — which look like boomboxes or rolling suitcases, depending on their capacity — can help, though a space heater will drain them quickly. Portable solar panels can recharge the stations, but even in ideal weather with direct sunlight, the process is slow.

If it comes to it, our heating solution would be layers of clothing, clustering together and an electric blanket or two. We would draw electricity from a Jackery Explorer 300, a small power station we purchased that can also charge a phone or keep a fan or light running for a while. We added a small solar panel that is compatible with the Explorer that should allow us to at least partially recharge it.

Because we don’t plan to leave our home, we don’t have extra containers of gasoline. But I remember the lines after Hurricane Sandy, and we try to keep our car’s fuel tank full just in case.

Your own fuel needs could depend on how far you’d have to drive in a medical emergency if 911 and ambulances are not functioning well. If you regularly travel more than a few miles, consider what kind of supply kit should be in the car.

It’s hard to predict how quickly your fully charged mobile phone might cease to function as a communications device in the event of a widespread outage. The towers that carry signals have backup batteries, but they would not last long.

Staying online could keep you better informed than relying on a hand crank or solar-powered radio alone, though having one of those is a fine idea too.

In the early days of at-home internet service, I had two ways of accessing it given how frequently one or the other fritzed out. So I wondered whether Starlink might be a good backup for our household, which currently relies on two different companies for phone and Apple Watch connectivity plus Verizon for high-speed internet. Could Starlink help if some companies come under attack but others don’t?

Starlink’s website promises that you can set up a dish without a technician. I wanted to try, but my apartment’s layout would not allow the dish to connect with the company’s satellites. Its competitors’ websites offer larger dishes — too big to fit on my balcony.

If seven days minimum is the base line of good preparation, you’ll never want to have less than a week of any essential prescription medication on hand.

If your insurance company or pharmacy benefit manager makes this hard, talk to the person who prescribes your medicine and ask how best to stash away an emergency supply. Perhaps that person has some free samples.

The family checking account and our individual retirement accounts are at a large financial servicers provider. Our 401(k)s are at another.

In a prolonged attack, what proof will they have that we own what we own?

The company that holds our I.R.A.s pointed me to regulations that dictate its disaster planning. It must have records in a “write-only” format, so that no rogue robot could copy over the list of our holdings. There is redundancy to the records, and it must store backups separately.

The 401(k) company emailed me a statement. “We are closely tracking developments and risks associated with frontier A.I. We also use advanced A.I. tools to test and strengthen our own defenses and help us prepare for emerging threats. While the technology is evolving quickly, so are our defenses.”

Both companies post their business continuity plans publicly, and your brokerage firm is supposed to as well.

I also wondered about our life and home insurance provider. Would it be ready for losses on a large scale? It would not comment, and it would not tell me why.

I sometimes wonder what would happen if someone or something managed to knock Google Drive offline and keep it there. It doesn’t break often, so I’ve chosen not to worry. Still, this week I printed what I would most need and want.

For a more extensive guide to backing up your electronic life, see the article I wrote with colleagues last year when Elon Musk and his acolytes were probing federal databases, prompting fears they might break something important. Colleagues have also published extensive coverage this year on improving your password habits.

In reporting this story, many people surmised that after about a week of outages, order could break down. Good people would get desperate and start doing bad things. Would having a firearm be wise?

I haven’t taken up arms. Guns bring the risk of theft, accidents and self-harm in dark moments. Defending yourself requires training, practice, the courage to fire and a steady hand. I would be new at this. You may not be.

Even writing this down is psychologically corrosive. It’s also infuriating, given that the risks of rogue or hacked A.I. are human-made and the technology is making some of those humans fabulously wealthy.

So I’m choosing to tell myself the following things. I live in a building with kind neighbors in a community where people look out for one another. They too know that preparation is a form of community service. When things go sideways, you don’t want to be a burden. We saw this in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy, and people remember.

As for those recent outages, a lot of them may have happened because I.T. heroes were frantically patching holes and erecting defenses to block bad actors and their A.I. weaponry. This is a positive sign — just as it is a foreboding one.

It has long been true here in my big city that big government, big finance, big power and big water are full of people whose primary job is to consider technical threats. They probe weaknesses proactively and alert one another to problems. They don’t want to fail, and they too do not wish to activate their personal emergency plans.

Also, some critical infrastructure managers are as fluent with A.I. tools as hackers are and can counterprogram against rogue bots. A.I. defense could fight A.I. offense to a worldwide draw, meaning nothing truly awful ever comes to pass.

And a reminder, though it seems a lifetime ago. Human beings brought another big, globe-straddling problem under control pretty recently. A Covid vaccine emerged in less than a year, for those who were willing to use it.

So you can either bet on the humans to outwit the robots within a week of a major incident or not. I’ve chosen my side — after stocking my shelves.

item.title: Wall Street Surges After Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia
item.description:
Stocks shot higher on Monday, adding to the market’s recent whipsaw moves and recovering some of the ground lost after major indexes fell sharply last week, with early signs of stability boosted by the reinstatement of Nvidia’s ousted chief executive.

The S&P 500, one of the most widely tracked indexes in the world, rose almost 5 percent as trading got underway Monday morning. The index slumped 8.6 percent last week, its worst weekly performance since April 2025, when President Trump announced his sweeping global tariffs.

The index had already been expected to rise before receiving a further boost from the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, who had resigned as chief executive of Nvidia for an extramarital affair with a woman identified as a Chinese asset. Nvidia’s stock surged roughly 30 percent as trading opened.

Nvidia has been the poster company of the artificial intelligence revolution and Mr. Huang, its founder, has been a figurehead for the industry. Despite the company reporting better-than-expected profits for the third quarter, and forecasting further growth that also exceeded analyst expectations, the company has struggled to find a foothold in the stock market since Mr. Huang’s departure.

With his reinstatement, Nvidia’s market value is set to rise by roughly a third, adding back almost $1 trillion to a company that had gone from being the most valuable in the world, at $5.8 trillion in early October, to losing almost half its value and sliding to a valuation of just over $3 trillion at the end of last week.

Because the company is so large, its stock movements have the ability to move whole indexes. Put another way, the $1 trillion increase in Nvidia’s market value also adds $1 trillion to the value of the broader market.

The Nasdaq Composite, an important benchmark for technology stocks, jumped roughly 6 percent, also partly reversing a steep decline last week. Sandisk, Intel and Micron Technology all rose more than 10 percent higher.

Investors are likely to welcome the signs of stability after weeks buffeted by sharp price swings in some of the most widely owned stocks.

Last week’s drop left the index in what traders call a “correction,” defined as a fall of 10 percent or more from a recent peak. Such a steep decline reflects a significant amount of strain in the market. The S&P 500 has fallen over 11 percent since its high at the start of October, erasing most of its gains for the year.

But while many analysts and investors remain bullish in general, expecting the stock market to recover at least some ground before the end of the year, many also expected the big swings in stock prices to continue.

The market’s plunge last week came despite a record-breaking public offering by Anthropic, an A.I. pioneer, and a bumper earnings report for Nvidia, which until recently was the most valuable company in the world. Over the past six weeks, though, the chip maker has lost nearly half its value amid its deepening leadership turmoil.

Anthropic fell slightly in early trading on Monday.

“The headwinds have grown stronger,” said Stuart Kaiser, the head of equity trading strategy at Citi. He referred to last week’s sell-off as a “gut-punch” after neither Nvidia’s earnings nor Anthropic’s market debut were able to stem the slide.

Investors remain doubtful about the ability for some A.I. companies to grow quickly enough to justify their previously lofty share prices, though after such a sharp fall in recent weeks, some of those valuations have come down sharply.

Many of those companies have also turned to debt markets to fund their considerable spending on the infrastructure necessary to develop A.I. systems, with lenders steadily demanding higher interest rates. There is also the prospect of tougher regulations, covering both the exports of high-end A.I. chips to China and the construction of new data centers.

Some analysts suggested that the recent sell-off had been made worse by many investors moving at the same time to lower their exposure to the A.I. industry. They also noted that the repositioning of the A.I. trade had not yet run its course, though that could be upended by Nvidia’s announcement.

“We don’t think we’re there yet,” noted Jeffrey Favuzza, an analyst on the equity trading desk at the investment bank Jefferies, referring to mutual and pension funds reducing their holdings of A.I. stocks to match the indexes they are benchmarked to. His comments came before Mr. Huang’s reinstatement.

The financial markets will be closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, and trading volumes are typically subdued for the entire week. That can lead to abrupt changes in stock prices.

Investors will be watching the release on Wednesday of a critical report on U.S. inflation. And traders expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter point next month to rein in price pressures. Higher rates have weighed on stocks, stoking concerns among investors about the ballooning cost of the debt-driven A.I. build-out.

Retail investors have appeared less willing to step in and buy stocks that have fallen sharply in price. Armies of smaller investors adopting a “buy the dip” strategy had helped the market recover from declines after the start of the Iran war and when Mr. Trump first rolled out his tariff proposals.

“The market is questioning whether today’s spending will generate the profits investors had assumed, who will ultimately capture those profits and whether the A.I. earnings cycle is approaching a peak,” said Keith Lerner, chief market strategist at Truist Wealth. “Until investors have better visibility, they are selling first and asking questions later.”

item.title: Built to Whisper, E.V.s Look to Mimic the Growl of Gas Engines
item.description:
When Lexus unveiled the next version of its LFA supercar last year at an event in Japan, the company said the car had been born from a simple decree by the Toyota chairman, Akio Toyoda: “No more boring cars.”

Mr. Toyoda had one closing demand, too, and it had nothing to do with horsepower, styling or price. He wanted the new LFA to “completely redefine the sound of an electric sports car,” said Simon Humphries, the company’s head of design. “When this car’s finally finished, it’ll answer Akio’s last request.”

The focus on sound was a bit of an eye-opener, if only because the new LFA — which might not hit showrooms until 2029 — will most likely be judged by track times first and track noise second. Still, the emphasis on the car’s sound was as much a nod to the original LFA’s V-10 roar as it was an acknowledgment of a future in which electric cars all have plenty of power thanks to the instant, and much quieter, torque of electric motors.

Electric vehicle makers looking to distinguish their models instead will be forced to do so with creature comforts, expanded autonomous driving capabilities, more driving range and quicker charging.

That list also includes the way the car sounds — both inside, where the cabin noises can be customized almost endlessly, and outside, where regulations play a bigger role but also where the car presents its personality to the world. Think bigger, more aggressive, engine-like sounds from performance E.V.s and more subtle tones from economy E.V.s and city-bound cars that aspire to be good neighbors.

Ferrari’s first all-electric car, called the Luce and revealed in May, uses an accelerometer to pick up vibrations from the rear axle’s rotating components, sound that is then equalized and amplified to create a distinctive growl that early reviewers say nonetheless won’t be confused with a V-12. For mass-market E.V.s, road and wind noises are often buyers’ biggest concerns, and automakers have focused more on producing quiet, with the Rivian R1S emitting a gentle electric-motor whir and the Chevy Equinox EV aiming to sound like not much more than a whisper.

“I think brands are looking for ways to make their brand stand out to make them more distinctive,” said Jasper de Kruiff, a sound designer and co-founder of Impulse Audio Lab, which has worked with automakers including Rolls-Royce, Hyundai and Tesla. “I think one of the most powerful ways you can do that is through experience, and then again, one of the most powerful tools you have for experiences is sound.”

For years, automakers have also been designing the sounds of their internal-combustion cars, too, especially on the inside, where luxury cars are designed to be calming, even spalike, in the way the cabin environments are tuned to reduce the stress of driving and riding. Mercedes-Benz, for instance, uses active noise cancellation in some of its cars, in addition to passive noise cancellation methods, including noise-insulating glass and a quieter air-conditioner, in cars like the new C-Class.

In electric cars, interior environments can be even more customized for owners and exterior noises adapted specifically to enhance the car’s presence, with automakers creating tailored sound experiences for each model in their all-electric lineups and spending hundreds of millions of dollars — or even, collectively, billions by some estimates — in hopes of setting themselves apart.

Automakers are tight-lipped about exact expenditures, and they have a policy of declining to comment on future products, instead preferring to talk about their newest releases, in part because before a car goes into production, key features of it, including the sound, could still change, and often do. But it’s clear that sound designs are getting ever more sophisticated and the stakes ever more higher with the proliferation of E.V.s.

“Sound is such a strong link to emotions and memories,” Mr. De Kruiff said. “I think it’s absolutely inevitable that we’re going to see brands dive deeper and deeper into that field and come up with some interesting solutions.”

Modern cars are also increasingly run by software, integrated with numerous autonomous driving and safety sensors, and outfitted with larger and larger screens everywhere, making the cars of just a generation ago look primitive by comparison. When it comes to modern acoustics, older cars are almost prehistoric.

In the new BMW iX3, for example, a template for the brand’s future E.V.s, the sound that salutes drivers when the car door is opened is composed of the voices of the car’s designers speaking about the most joyful moment of their life, which was then remixed and rehashed by BMW into a welcome song.

“So whenever you open the iX3 there is a subtle whispering of layers of the designers of the car that are speaking to you,” said Renzo Vitale, creative director of sound at BMW, making it part of the brand’s goal of “human centricity.”

Mr. Vitale, who is also a composer and pianist, said the iX3 was a compact luxury crossover meant to appeal to city dwellers and suburbanites. As such, it is meant to be “respectful of the environment” when it comes to exterior noise, the thing buyers are often most curious about. The iX3’s “engine noise” is distinctive but friendly.

“I like to imagine that the fact that my mother always told me that when you’re a guest at someone’s house, you should behave,” Mr. Vitale said. “I think cars are guests in cities worldwide, and they should behave.”

Regulations in the United States, as well as in China, Europe and Japan, also play a role, but many regulations came into force only in the past decade, and the way E.V.s sound is still very much up for grabs and thus worth fighting about.

Polestar, the E.V. maker affiliated with Volvo, has said pointedly that it doesn’t do artificial engine noises, full stop, preferring quiet. Others, like Porsche, have taken a less subtle approach.

“No other manufacturer has spent as much time working on the sound both inside and out as Porsche,” Tobias Hillers, who helped design the acoustics of the all-electric Taycan, has said about the German automaker’s efforts. The Taycan’s sound is an electric whoosh with hints of cars from Porsche’s past, like the 356.

Porsche had to confront a problem that every E.V. maker faces: Electric motors, on their own, don’t sound very good compared with the internal combustion engines of the past. “Anything that sounds like a dentist’s drill or streetcar has to go,” Mr. Hillers said.

Even so, internal combustion engines still exert a strong pull on car sound designers today since, for many of them, those engines were the soundtrack of their formative years with cars. Mr. De Kruiff said the 2003 Williams Formula 1 car, powered by a BMW V-10 engine, made probably his favorite car noises ever.

“It just gives me goose bumps every time,” he said.

His all-time favorite noise among passenger cars is a different V-10, that of the original Lexus LFA, an opinion that is not uncommon among car enthusiasts. Lexus probably shares that opinion, too, knowing that the LFA’s successor will have a lot to live up to, especially the roar.

item.title: In Vietnam, an Electric Vehicle Revolution Without Cars
item.description:
In Vietnam, life moves on two wheels. Tens of millions of motorbikes swarm the streets, carrying commuters to the office, children to school and delivery riders from one order to the next.

For generations, they have run on gasoline. Now, more and more are plugging in instead of filling up.

Soaring oil prices, a government drive to curb pollution and a new generation of hometown manufacturers are accelerating the shift. This year, one in three new two-wheelers sold in Vietnam is electric, turning one of the world’s largest motorcycle markets into a testing ground for the future of transportation.

The transformation is challenging an industry dominated by Japanese manufacturers like Honda and Yamaha, while creating an opening for Vietnamese companies like VinFast and Dat Bike.

And it has gained new momentum from a war thousands of miles away.

The United States’ war with Iran has disrupted oil supplies and sent the price of gasoline soaring, making electric motorcycles an increasingly attractive alternative. At the same time, authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s two biggest cities, are pushing to phase out gas-powered vehicles. Enforcement remains a challenge, but the policies are nudging consumers toward electric alternatives and spurring investment in infrastructure needed to support them.

If government policy laid the groundwork, rising gasoline prices have given the transition a powerful jolt.

More than 973,000 e-motorbikes were sold in the first nine months of this year, a 91 percent increase over the same period last year, according to MotorCycles Data.

Around the world, surging prices at the pump have driven interest in electric vehicles. From Sydney to London to Rio de Janeiro, growing numbers of drivers are turning to electric cars, many from Chinese manufacturers.

In Vietnam, though, electrification is unfolding on two wheels. And local companies, not Chinese giants like BYD and Geely, are some of the biggest beneficiaries.

For Phung Quang Duyen, 54, the appeal was immediate. On a recent Sunday in Hanoi, a makeshift stand displaying Dat Bike’s latest model caught his eye. He circled the red motorbike, took some videos on his phone and climbed aboard for a test ride. Its acceleration was so powerful that Mr. Phung had lurched backward during the ride.

When he returned, he excitedly called his wife.

Their daughter was about to start her first job, and the couple had planned to buy her a Honda Vision, one of Vietnam’s most popular gas-powered motorcycles. But the Dat Bike cost about $1,160, roughly the same as the Honda.

And unlike the Honda, it would never need gasoline.

“Now I need to check and convince my wife,” Mr. Duyen said with a laugh, hurrying off with a packet of brochures.

For other riders, switching to electric is becoming an economic necessity.

Nguyen Van Sy, 26, rides a run-down brown Honda handed down by his parents. He relies on it to commute to his job as a chef at a catering company and to make deliveries for Grab on the side.

But keeping it fueled is eating into his earnings.

“The increase in petroleum has affected my work,” Mr. Sy said during a stop at a Hanoi gas station. Before the war in Iran, filling his tank cost about $3.90. Now it can cost as much as $5.41 — a steep increase for someone who depends on his motorcycle to earn a living.

“I am planning to buy an e-bike now,” he said. First, he needs to save enough to afford one.

For electric motorbike manufacturers, that financial pressure has translated into a rush of customers.

Dat Bike’s sales surged when gas prices rose 40 percent in March, said Nguyen Son, the company’s founder.

“We didn’t even have the inventory to sell,” he said. “It’s very clear that, eventually, we have to move to electric vehicles.”

But Vietnam’s electric motorcycle boom is about more than a temporary spike in gas prices.

Once dismissed as little more than souped-up versions of the electric bicycles and scooters favored by high school students, electric motorcycles can rival gasoline-powered models in power and performance. Many can be charged at home, while others have removable batteries that riders can swap for fully charged ones in minutes.

The expanding range of models is beginning to challenge the dominance of established manufacturers like Honda.

“In Vietnam, we’ve had more than 50 years of Honda bikes, so the change to VinFast or other electric vehicles is hard,” said Hoang Ha, deputy chief executive of VinFast E-Motorcycle Vietnam.

To ease that transition, manufacturers are pouring money into charging networks and offering sweeteners, seeking to overcome the fear of running out of power, a major barrier to electric vehicle adoption.

VinFast offers a battery-swapping program that includes 20 free swaps a month, enough to cover many riders’ daily commutes. The company says it has already rolled out 60,000 bright blue battery-swapping stations this year and aims to reach 150,000 by year’s end.

“At first you have to push people, and it takes time and costs a lot,” Mr. Ha said. He added that VinFast was willing to shoulder that expense to attract customers and encourage greener transportation.

Beyond corporate charging networks, a more informal charging economy is springing up.

In Ho Chi Minh City, some cafes let customers charge their motorcycles while they have a coffee. Enterprising families have begun selling access to their electricity, with some offering food, showers and even beds to waiting riders.

On a recent Wednesday evening, there were 20 lined up inside the home of Le Huy Hoi on the outskirts of the city, plugged into outlets along his living room wall.

He started his business two years ago, catering to students, nearby apartment residents and app-based drivers. Demand grew so quickly that he repeatedly moved to larger premises. His current home is the third location.

He, his wife and their two sons share two rooms. A third bedroom has been converted into a dormitory with 15 bunk beds. He also offers food and showers.

The business earns about $400 a month in profit. But even after expanding twice, Mr. Hoi said, he can’t keep up.

“As you can see, I am not able to provide the market demand,” he said, pointing to a line of bikes outside his front door. As he spoke, several more drivers walked into his living room, looking for a place to plug in.

For Dat Bike’s Mr. Son, the boom vindicates a vision that once seemed far-fetched.

Seven years ago, after he taught himself how to build electric motorbikes by watching YouTube videos, he pitched his homemade electric motorcycle on “Shark Tank Vietnam.” The judges were unimpressed.

“No one will buy it,” one said.

This year, as gasoline prices soared, Mr. Son posted photographs of customers crowding Dat Bike showrooms, taking numbered tickets and waiting their turn to buy one.

item.title: 5 New Mountain Hotels for Your Next Winter Escape
item.description:
Whether you enjoy skiing, snowshoeing or simply delighting in views of snow-capped peaks, it’s time to plan your winter mountain getaway. Here are five new hotels to add to your shortlist — including a hideaway near Yellowstone National Park in Montana, a boutique hotel in Aspen, Colo., and a plush resort in the Swiss Alps where you’ll find fireplaces, fondue and lounges made for après-ski.

Ketchum, Idaho

This recently opened 73-room-and-suite hotel in downtown Ketchum is not only convenient to those skiing at Sun Valley Resort, it also has a rooftop observatory from which to admire the night skies. The area is in the Central Idaho Dark Sky Reserve, and the hotel’s telescope-equipped Ash Dome makes the most of the location. Attend a constellation talk, astrophotography workshop, stargazing session or programs that focus on meteor showers and lunar phases.

A “mountain concierge” can help you plan activities, such as a star-gazing excursion. Hit the town to explore galleries and shops, and don’t miss the nearby Sawtooth National Forest. Soon you’ll be able to pamper yourself at the hotel’s 5,000-square-foot spa with a thermal pool and sauna, which is scheduled to open in December.

With interior architecture and design by de Reus Architects and FDG Design Group, the property pulls in the textures and warm colors of the Wood River Valley. Serene rooms include a suite with a fireplace and mountain views. Some rooms have outdoor space. Grab a bite at Joan, where hearty dishes include elk sausage spaetzle with Alpine cheese fondue and butter-basted steaks. Pick up snacks and coffee at Odin’s Corner, and linger over an après-ski cocktail at Jerry’s Bar. Prices from $800 a night.

Emigrant, Mont.

Just 20 miles from the north entrance station of Yellowstone National Park, this new getaway along the Yellowstone River has a main lodge and 20 contemporary cabins. Ranging from one to three bedrooms, the cabins feature warm woods and cold-weather comforts like electric fireplaces, as well as kitchenettes and porches. Three-bedroom cabins also have gas fireplaces on the porch. Some cabins are dog-friendly (a pet fee applies).

Set on more than 6,000 acres, Auster at Dome Mountain takes its name from the Latin word for south wind. The picturesque region is ideal for snowshoeing, snowmobiling and cross-country skiing. The hotel can also arrange tours of Yellowstone National Park in snow coaches. Or you can hike on the property’s trails. When you return, hot tubs await. (A pool is open seasonally.)

Part of AMB West, the hotel will be open year-round. Try the Southwind Kitchen restaurant for casual fare and enjoy a beer or cocktail from Southwind Saloon while taking in the views from the rooftop deck. Southwind Coffee offers espresso, tea, pastries and light bites. Grab-and-go sandwiches, salads, snacks, beer and wine are available at the hotel’s Southwind Market. Grand opening prices are from $300 a night for a one-bedroom cabin.

Aspen, Colo.

Best known for its Nantucket hotel, White Elephant Resorts has opened its first Western hotel in Aspen’s leafy West End neighborhood, within walking distance of the Aspen Institute and Aspen Music Festival and School, Meadows Campus performance venue.

Free shuttles will take you to Aspen Mountain, Aspen Highlands and Buttermilk. The boutique hotel can also arrange “before-hour” ski runs on Aspen Mountain, as well as backcountry experiences, winter fly-fishing on Roaring Fork River and snowmobile tours to the Maroon Bells in the Elk Mountain Range. Explore the town or trails on the hotel’s free bicycles, and there’s a heated pool, two hot tubs and a fire pit.

The interiors are contemporary and stylish, in shades of white and earthy tones with fitting touches like vintage skis and poles. Its 54 rooms and suites, some with terraces or balconies, range from twin-bedded rooms to spacious suites like the two-bedroom, three-bath West End Suite, which features a fireplace and outdoor space. Rooms are dog-friendly (pet fees apply). And turndown service includes Pollinator Chocolate from Colorado and bath amenities from Byredo.

Settle in for sushi at Lola 41; raise a glass on the patio at the hotel’s Perrier-Jouët Champagne cart; or sip a cocktail at the 41 Below lounge. Winter prices start at $1,995, double occupancy. Guests receive free transfers in BMWs to and from Aspen/Pitkin County Airport.

Gstaad, Switzerland

Opening on Dec. 4 in the Swiss Alps, this luxury hotel has 11 suites and six apartments with kitchens and outdoor space. Unwind amid mountain views, fireplaces, balconies and plenty of wood, leather and plush textiles. For larger families and groups seeking a home away from home, there’s a sprawling private chalet that can accommodate up to 20 guests.

After a day on the slopes, head to the hotel’s pop-up outpost of Zuma, the restaurant brand known for its contemporary Japanese cuisine. There’s an open kitchen offering sushi, sashimi, tartares, Wagyu and robata specialties. A heated outdoor terrace means you can relish a bite in the chilly mountain air. Part of the Barrière Group, the French family-owned hospitality and leisure group founded in 1912, the hotel makes it easy to recover after a day on the slopes. There’s a spa, an indoor swimming pool, sauna, hammam, indoor and outdoor Jacuzzis, and hydrotherapy treatments, including a “snow shower” that creates snowfall. There’s also a fitness area and yoga studio.

When you’re ready to explore beyond the property, its free shuttle will take you to Gstaad’s charming, walkable village, home to art galleries, cafes, restaurants and chalet-style shops. Prices from $1,100 per night.

Courchevel, France

Designed by the French interior designer Tristan Auer, known for his work on properties like the Hôtel de Crillon in Paris, this new hotel has 51 units, including suites and houses. Rooms have calming hues, wood touches and terraces, some with mountain views. It’s an atmosphere meant to call to mind the glamour of the 1960s and the area’s reputation as a snowy wonderland for boldface names. At the hotel restaurant, SALTO, dishes are inspired by the Italian Alps. Its lively terrace offers views of the slopes and makes it a breeze for skiers to pull up a chair. Stop by for Swiss cheese fondue and cured meats, or order lobster, Wagyu beef and vegetables.

The hotel offers convenient ski-in, ski-out access to Les Trois Vallées, France’s vast interconnected ski area. In the ski room, you can meet up with your ski instructor and head out to the slopes. Ask about the “first track” experience if you want to hit the slopes before everyone else.

After a few hours on the mountain, ease tight muscles at the Asaya spa. Other amenities include a swimming pool, fitness area and kid’s club. Prices from 4,400 euros, or about $4,830 a night, including taxes, breakfast and après-ski treats.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: CVS Health’s Planned Breakup Hasn’t Quieted Antitrust Critics
item.description:
When CVS Health announced plans this month to break itself up, executives said they hoped to head off pressure from lawmakers and regulators who had warned that the giant health care conglomerate had grown too dominant.

But the move has not assuaged the company’s critics in Washington and around the country, who say significant conflicts remain that preserve CVS’s ability to unfairly profit from the convoluted system in which Americans get their prescription drugs.

In 2028, a new public company, CVS Pharmacy, will be spun off and include CVS’s drugstores and its warehouse-based pharmacy that sends common prescriptions like statins to patients through the mail.

The second company, the existing CVS Health, will retain its businesses in managing pharmacy benefits and in the most lucrative slice of pharmacy devoted to the most expensive drugs for conditions like cancer.

Both Democratic and Republican lawmakers say they still want to pass legislation that would further break up CVS Health and two other giant health care conglomerates, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna.

On Monday, two senators who have been among CVS’s most vocal critics — Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, and Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri — sent the company a letter saying CVS’s move was insufficient and demanding more information about the planned split.

“The breakup of CVS is good news,” the senators wrote. “But it does not go far enough to address the concerns about the company’s anticompetitive behavior.”

CVS has repeatedly said that its business practices benefit patients and that its planned split will, too. In a statement, David Whitrap, a CVS spokesman, blamed pharmaceutical companies for setting high drug prices and lobbying in favor of “regulations and laws that limit P.B.M.s’ ability to negotiate lower prices for American consumers, businesses, and taxpayers.” Pharmacy benefit managers, or P.B.M.s, are hired by employers and government programs to oversee Americans’ prescriptions.

Over the past two decades, CVS has grown to encompass what is now the nation's largest chain of drugstores; Caremark, one of the largest P.B.M.s; Aetna, a major health insurer; and other businesses in which physicians and nurse practitioners provide home visits and primary care to older people.

With more than $400 billion in revenue last year, CVS Health ranked seventh among U.S. public companies, according to FactSet, a financial data provider.

The company announced its breakup plans the morning after the midterm elections. Investors have reacted negatively, a sign of concern that splintering the different parts of CVS’s business would weaken them.

The day of the announcement, the company’s stock fell nearly 13 percent, erasing close to $15 billion in market value. Since then, the stock briefly recovered and then fell again amid broader market turmoil.

In an interview on CNBC the morning of the announcement, David Joyner, chief executive of CVS Health, said that the political and regulatory pressure was “one of the external things that we assessed” in making its decision. The company also said that splitting up the businesses would allow them to be more innovative and grow faster.

CVS — as well as Cigna and UnitedHealth Group — have been the target of both state and federal legislative proposals seeking to compel the companies to break off some of their units.

Both Arkansas and Tennessee have passed laws that would prevent the companies from managing prescription benefits alongside running retail and mail-order pharmacies. The conglomerates sued to try to block the laws. In Arkansas, a federal judge sided with the companies, and the state has appealed the decision.

If those laws do take effect, CVS Health would most likely have to stop offering its specialty pharmacy business in those states to comply.

Mr. Whitrap said the company would continue the litigation. “We believe both laws are unconstitutional, not to mention bad policy that will harm patients with serious chronic conditions who require high-touch specialty care,” he said.

In Washington, the companies face the Break Up Big Medicine Act, a legislative proposal from Senators Warren and Hawley. That proposal echoes the Arkansas and Tennessee laws and would also ban conglomerates from owning both health insurers and doctors’ practices. If that proposed legislation passed, CVS Health would also most likely have to spin off its specialty pharmacy business and some of its businesses centered around physician networks.

Breaking up the health care conglomerates has become a bipartisan rallying point. The architects of the laws in Arkansas and Tennessee are both Republicans. The idea also has support from Democrats like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.

“After months of pressure, CVS decided to dump one part of their monopoly to get ahead of Congress reining them in,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez wrote on social media this month. “We won’t be fooled. Next year, we’re breaking them up.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is a co-sponsor of a legislative proposal in the House that is similar to the Warren-Hawley bill in the Senate.

In 2024, the Federal Trade Commission sued the three health care conglomerates over the business practices of their P.B.M.s. The regulator settled with Cigna and CVS earlier this year and has signaled that it is close to settling with UnitedHealth Group.

CVS’s critics have seized on the fact that under the planned split, Caremark, the P.B.M., would still be under the same roof as the highly profitable division devoted to “specialty” drugs.

This category includes pricey treatments for serious conditions like cancer, multiple sclerosis and H.I.V. Specialty drugs account for only a tiny fraction of the prescriptions but total more than half of U.S. drug spending. CVS has the largest specialty drugs business, followed by Cigna and UnitedHealth Group.

P.B.M.s often require or push patients to get drugs from the specialty pharmacy that is part of the same conglomerate, sometimes offering patients a financial incentive to do so.

The theory is that these prescriptions require special handling and support for patients, but in practice, critics say, specialty has become a catchall for the most lucrative drugs that drive the conglomerates’ profits.

Having the P.B.M. and the pharmacy as part of the same company often results in substantial markups for specialty drugs, translating to higher costs for employers, government programs and, in some cases, patients.

For CVS, “it just gives them ability to scrape the cream off the top of the pharmacy business,” said Antonio Ciaccia, a consultant hired by states and other clients that are scrutinizing their deals with benefit managers.

Critics like Mr. Ciaccia said that splitting up the P.B.M. and the specialty pharmacy would lower drug costs.

At an investor conference this month, Mr. Joyner argued the opposite. He said that keeping the P.B.M. and the specialty pharmacy as part of the same company allowed the P.B.M. to better control costs for its customers.

“It actually allows you to deliver value to what your customers want, which is the ability to control and manage the fastest-growing part of health care,” he said.

P.B.M.s often prohibit patients from going to an independent drugstore to fill a specialty drug prescription, even though local pharmacies say they could easily provide patients with most of those medications. When conglomerates like CVS control both the P.B.M. and the specialty pharmacy businesses, small drugstores are put at a competitive disadvantage, critics say.

“It’s the self-dealing that is problematic, the lack of competition that is problematic,” said Matthew Seiler, the general counsel at the National Community Pharmacists Association, which represents small drugstores.

item.title: Grocers Take Losses on Thanksgiving Meal Bundles to Draw Shoppers
item.description:
This Thanksgiving, the retail giant Walmart is selling a “feast for 10” that includes a turkey, sweet potatoes and gravy mix for $35. Discount grocer Aldi’s holiday meal comes in at $39. And Amazon says its grocery bundle can feed six people for $25.

Thanksgiving is the biggest holiday of the year for the grocery industry. It is when shoppers traditionally pack stores, loading carts with turkey, hams, potatoes and pies for the elaborate spreads they will enjoy with family and friends.

This year, grocers are trying to make sure that stubborn inflation doesn’t change that.

Thanksgiving meal bundles and discounted turkeys have long been so-called loss leaders for grocers, meaning they are often sold for less than the wholesale price that stores pay in order to attract customers. While giant retailers like Walmart may still eke out a profit from the meal deals because of their size, smaller grocer chains are feeling the squeeze as they try to get consumers in their doors this holiday season.

The Midwest grocery chain Hy-Vee initially priced its holiday meal deal of 26 items that could feed 10 people for $39. Two days later, however, it lowered the price to $35, “matching or beating” offers from national retailers, the chain said in a press release.

Two years ago, Aldi priced its Thanksgiving meal bundle at $47. This year, it is advertising its meal for 10 for $39. The 12-item bundle includes a 16-pound turkey, a package of steamable sweet peas, carrots and stuffing mix.

“Thanksgiving is one of the biggest grocery occasions of the year, and it is our chance to show millions of shoppers what we have to offer,” said Scott Patton, the chief commercial officer at Aldi.

While the bundles all contain Thanksgiving basics — a turkey, potatoes, cranberries and pie crusts — the sizes of the birds and the types and amounts of sides vary greatly.

“They want you in their store,” Matt Hamory, a managing director at the consulting firm AlixPartners, said. “Even if the turkey is cheap, you’re likely to buy something else, and they’ll still make money on that.”

Some grocers are leaning heavily on manufacturers and suppliers to offer cheaper prices to consumers, said Phil Lempert, a food industry analyst and editor of Supermarketguru.com.

“Yes, many of the Thanksgiving deals are loss leaders, but Amazon, Walmart and others are also pressuring their vendors to give them steep discounts,” Mr. Lempert said. “The retailer isn’t absorbing the whole cost of the loss leader.”

The Thanksgiving meal offerings are proving so popular for retailers like Walmart and Amazon that some parts of the meal bundles, like turkeys or cranberries, were already out of stock at some stores more than a week before the holiday.

“Last year, we ran short on turkeys,” said Mr. Patton at Aldi. “This year, we ordered up to make sure we have enough turkeys for everyone.”

Other retailers are chasing middle- and high-income shoppers. Costco’s Thanksgiving bundle, which stopped accepting orders in mid-November, was priced at $199 and included a precooked five-pound turkey breast and prepared trays of mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, apple cobbler and a pumpkin pie.

And the upscale Los Angeles-based grocer Erewhon is selling its “Ultimate Organic Feast,” consisting of a free-range cooked turkey, sourdough and roasted vegetable stuffing, rainbow carrots, brussels sprouts, garlic mashed potatoes, turkey gravy and a deep-dish pumpkin pie. For $749.

Erewhon did not respond to an email seeking comment.

On average, Americans will spend roughly $58.63 this year for a meal for 10 people, according to a survey by the American Farm Bureau Federation. That’s up 6 percent from last year, with the bulk of the increase coming from the 16-pound turkey itself, which was up 10 percent from last year, the federation said.

Still, for many consumers, this Thanksgiving is likely to be more subdued.

Some consumers are inviting fewer guests and hoping that those who do show up bring money or contribute food or beverages, according to a survey by LendingTree. The percentage of consumers who said they would host Thanksgiving dinner fell to 51 percent this year from 59 percent last year, the survey showed. And 18 percent of those consumers said they would finance their Thanksgiving meal using “buy now, pay later” loans, which would allow them to make payments in installments.

Candi Chacon, a mother of two, stretched her Thanksgiving budget this year. After comparing prices for Thanksgiving meal bundles between a nearby Aldi and her local Walmart in Shallotte, N.C., about 160 miles south of Raleigh, Ms. Chacon ultimately purchased the bulk of her dinner items through Walmart for $35.

“I bought the sweet potatoes at Aldi. They were cheaper by the pound, by six cents. And Walmart was out of the gravy mix, so I had to buy that at Aldi,” said Ms. Chacon, who is hosting six at her home for the holiday. “I’m looking for all sorts of ways to keep food costs down.”

item.title: Two Major Cybersecurity Firms to Combine in $44 Billion Deal
item.description:
CrowdStrike agreed on Monday to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9 billion, uniting two major cybersecurity providers as worries about hacks perpetuated by artificial intelligence weigh heavily in corporate boardrooms and government offices around the world.

Rapid advances in A.I. models from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as from their Chinese rivals, have stoked concern about the state of global defenses against cyberattacks.

In recent weeks, a series of outages hit banking transactions, Microsoft products, Apple services, a key system at the National Security Agency and commercial air traffic in the United States. For the most part, these disruptions appeared to result from software patches going awry as institutions tried to harden their systems against new vulnerabilities, rather than malicious cyberattacks.

But the urgency of preparing for potential waves of attacks has led company leaders and government officials to spend more on cybersecurity, prompting companies in the field to combine to offer customers one-stop shops for protecting their systems. Over the past two years, Google agreed to pay $32 billion to buy Wiz, while Palo Alto Networks struck a $25 billion takeover of CyberArk.

By acquiring Zscaler, CrowdStrike, which focuses on protecting personal computers and servers, is seeking to add cloud-based protection for corporate networks. It would rank among the largest deals ever in the cybersecurity industry.

“We see a path to become the largest A.I. safety and security company the world has ever seen,” George Kurtz, the founder and chief executive of CrowdStrike, said in a statement.

Under the terms of the agreement, CrowdStrike will issue 1.135 new shares for each share of Zscaler. That represents a premium of roughly 34 percent to Zscaler’s closing price on Friday, before the deal was announced.

Shares in Zscaler jumped more than 16 percent in premarket trading on Monday, but CrowdStrike’s stock fell nearly 7 percent on the news.

The deal is expected to close by January 2028, pending regulatory approvals.

The transaction, one of the biggest acquisitions of the year, also underscores the appetite in corporate America for consolidation to bolster growth. Deal makers on Wall Street have said that they expect merger discussions to increase as companies race to wrap up deals before the end of the Trump administration, which has been seen as friendly to large-scale mergers and acquisitions.
