item.title: Can Jensen Huang Return to Nvidia?
item.description:
Andrew here. Is this the week the market hits an inflection point?

Last week’s rout exposed major fault lines: the midterm election’s regulatory threat to data center expansion; tightening export controls on Nvidia’s China sales; and a liquidity drain prompted by Anthropic’s mega-I.P.O. Just as worrying, a strong earnings season has done little to restore investor confidence.

The defining question for Wall Street right now: Are we entering a long-lasting bear market, or is this just a painful, temporary reset? More below.

Efforts by a vocal group of Silicon Valley moguls (backed by President Trump) to get Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as C.E.O. appeared to gain steam over the weekend after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent seemed to soften his public opposition to the idea.

But new revelations about the Chinese woman involved in the Huang scandal may have muddied the waters again.

“Jensen is on the outside now,” Bessent said on Sunday on the CBS News program “Face the Nation” when asked about his previous demand that Nvidia’s board “go outside the company” to find a permanent chief.

Bessent added that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the chip executive who U.S. intelligence official determined was a spy for China, was essentially a “canard.” The biggest issue, the Treasury secretary said, was determining how Nvidia chips ended up in China despite restrictions on those sales. He suggested that the buck stopped below the C.E.O.: “What were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?”

Bessent’s comments came after repeated support for Huang by Trump, who implored Nvidia’s board on Friday to give the former C.E.O. “a second chance,” and wrote on social media on Sunday that it would be “the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.”

Some pro-Huang tech moguls took heart from Bessent’s comments: “Progress,” Travis Kalanick, the Uber co-founder who has publicly demanded the reinstatement of Huang, wrote on social media.

Shares in Nvidia were up 8.6 percent in premarket trading.

Could a new report change that? The Times reports, citing people familiar with U.S. intelligence reports, that Alice Huang had been in touch with an official at China’s top spy agency for more than a year — at least partly overlapping with her affair with Huang. (Kang Wei, a business associate of Alice Huang’s who was often introduced as her husband, also worked with the same agency, the people said.)

The pressure to reinstate Huang hangs heavily on Nvidia’s board. An independent review of Huang is underway, even as the company’s new chairman, Harvey Jones, declared last week that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.”

Rehiring Huang before the review is complete could add to the board’s legal headaches, if the inquiry finds any wrongdoing. (DealBook hears that what pushed the board to oust Huang was a report about another affair involving a direct report.)

Many bettors on prediction markets are increasingly wagering that Huang will return: The implied odds of him becoming Nvidia’s next C.E.O. have hit 17 percent on Kalshi and 19 percent on Polymarket, putting him in the lead. (The previous front-runner, Rene Haas, just agreed to stay on at the chip designer Arm through 2033.)

The stakes of the Nvidia leadership question are huge. The chip maker’s processors power a majority of the artificial intelligence world’s leading applications, while its balance sheet is single-handedly propping up a huge portion of A.I. start-ups. (Though Wall Street is increasingly divided over the wisdom of the trillion-dollar chip financing boom — more on that below.)

Climate talks collapse. COP31, this year’s United Nations climate summit, broke down without a final agreement. The European Union and small countries vulnerable to climate disasters rejected a proposal that blocked any mention of fossil fuels, a root cause of global warming. The impasse underscores the tension in efforts to transition to more renewable energy sources as President Trump and oil-producing giants such as Saudi Arabia promote fossil fuels.

An Anthropic researcher claims to have deciphered a major mathematics problem. A mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpoge, said he had used Claude to solve the super-complicated Riemann hypothesis. If the claim is verified, it will be the latest remarkable advance by artificial intelligence in the field of mathematics this year. Speaking of numbers, Wall Street expects that the bonds Anthropic sells to fund its $900 billion spending commitments to be rated at junk.

Trump finds an issue where he can work with Democrats. Trump said he would collaborate with Democrats to cap interest and fees on credit cards, an issue long pushed by Senator Elizabeth Warren, the Massachusetts Democrat set to be the new chair of the Banking Committee. (The banking industry claimed that such a move would deny credit to millions of people with poor credit ratings.) The bipartisan gesture came as the Democrats won their 258th seat in the House with the election of Chuck Hubbard in North Carolina, clinching their largest majority since 1992.

CrowdStrike acquires a rival. The cybersecurity firm agreed to buy Zscaler for about $44 billion in stock. Shares in CrowdStrike fell more than 6 percent in premarket trading on the news. Analysts are wondering if the tie-up presages a string of deals in the sector, as advanced A.I. models make it increasingly easy for hackers to break into corporate and government systems.

The Nasdaq Composite looks set to rebound on Monday. But Wall Street is still fretting about the artificial intelligence trade after Anthropic’s record-breaking I.P.O. fizzled amid a huge sell-off last week in tech stocks.

Investors are worried about the economics of the A.I. buildout, including the financing and life span of A.I. chips — the brunt of which come from Nvidia — that power the technology. Against that backdrop, two Wall Street heavyweights, Apollo Global Management and Ares Management, have staked out drastically different positions, Niko Gallogly reports.

Trillions of dollars are expected to flow into A.I. over the next several years. For every dollar spent, about 60 cents will go toward chips, according to McKinsey.

But Ares Management sees major risks in those investments. The firm recently argued in its In the Gaps newsletter that chips were “one the fastest-depreciating assets we can name” and that “financing markets have the shortest track record and least experience,” underwriting them.

“I, for one, personally do not know how to underwrite the decline in depreciation curves on that type of technology,” Michael Arougheti, the C.E.O. of Ares, told analysts last month.

Apollo’s C.E.O., Marc Rowan, called out the Ares newsletter in the firm’s earnings call this month: “Not to make fun of the Ares publication, but you have to mind the gap,” he said when discussing A.I.-related investment risk.

Apollo has gone all in on chips, helping to arrange several multi-billion-dollar financing deals. That includes roughly $44 billion for SpaceX, what the firms called the largest such deal on record. It carries substantial security provisions for lenders:

SpaceX has agreed to pay back the loan even if the GPUs fail, meaning that lenders are underwriting SpaceX’s corporate payment risk rather than hardware performance.

The loan has a maturity of roughly five years and is paid off over the life of the loan rather than at the end.

“Credits across the A.I. ecosystem aren’t inherently good or bad,” Joanna Rose, the global head of corporate communications at Apollo, told DealBook. “It comes down to structure, collateral and the partner behind the obligation.”

Goldman Sachs, BlackRock and KKR all participated in the roughly $44 billion SpaceX deal. Blackstone, which is helping to finance a $63 billion loan for Anthropic to purchase Broadcom chips, is also a major player.

Apollo joined Blackstone and others in announcing in August a deal to help finance Nvidia’s customers’ chip purchases to the tune of $500 billion. To date, no money has changed hands, The Wall Street Journal reports.

Ares isn’t sitting out the A.I. trade altogether. The company is focused instead on financing data center structures, or shells, and powering those buildings.

chart of the day

How bad was the stock market rout last week? The S&P 500 fell more than 8 percent, its worst one-week performance since the Liberation Day sell-off in April 2025, pushing the benchmark index into correction territory. The futures market points to a decent bounce on Monday. But the Cboe Volatility Index — Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge — has been trending in the wrong direction lately, potentially signaling more turbulence ahead.

The financier Mark Walter shot to the public eye after he began buying up stakes in prominent sports assets like the Dodgers and the Lakers, deals that have since been examined by federal prosecutors and the S.E.C.

One of those transactions, the takeover in 2012 of the Dodgers, added a notable sports figure to Walter’s orbit: Magic Johnson, an N.B.A. Hall of Famer who was intent on business success after his pro basketball career.

Walter, who asked Johnson to join the Dodgers ownership group, made the basketball star a compelling pitch: “Mark Walter said, ‘You don’t need them. Come to me for funding,’” Johnson told the Economic Club of Chicago last year, according to The Wall Street Journal. “‘So that’s what I do.’”

That made Johnson a billionaire — but has also put him under scrutiny for his ties to Walter, The Journal reports:

In 2014, Johnson struck a deal to buy a majority stake in Iowa-based EquiTrust, one of Walter’s Guggenheim-run insurance companies. In the years since, Walter’s insurers invested hundreds of millions of dollars into Johnson’s investment funds and lent around $2 billion to expand the retired sports star’s insurance group.

Owners also profited. EquiTrust’s assets more than doubled under Johnson’s ownership to $36 billion by the end of last year, and it paid out $390 million in net dividends from 2015 to 2025. Johnson’s portion was around $234 million, based on his share of the company.

During this time, there also was substantial growth in loans to companies tied to Walter. Those loans eventually accounted for a third of EquiTrust’s assets, The Journal found. Arizona, where the company is now based, has a limit of 10 percent for a single borrower.

By 2025, Johnson had invested $12.3 billion from EquiTrust Life Insurance into enterprises controlled by or linked to Walter (who also held a stake in EquiTrust), according to The Journal. Johnson hasn’t been accused of wrongdoing.

Deals

“Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual I.P.O. process, chafing some bankers” (Reuters)

Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award-winner, reportedly agreed to a record-breaking nine-year, $450 million deal with Steve Cohen’s New York Mets. (The Athletic)

Firmus Grid, an Australian firm backed by Nvidia that builds artificial intelligence data centers, is said to be considering a roughly $1.5 billion bond offering after it called off its I.P.O. (Bloomberg)

Politics, policy and regulation

Pure Lithium, a start-up that makes lithium metal batteries, reportedly rejected a request in July from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to sell the U.S. government a majority stake. (Reuters)

Bayer’s court battles over the weedkiller Roundup took a major turn, after a Missouri judge approved a $7.25 billion settlement to end tens of thousands of U.S. lawsuits that claimed that Roundup caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma. (NYT)

Best of the rest

In the enduring dead-not-dead debate: The penny is a goner; documentary films, however, are not. (NYT, WaPo)

“Oxford and MIT Didn’t Bite. So Ken Griffin Took His Miami Campus Elsewhere.” (WSJ)

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
Nvidia said on Monday that it reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive less than two weeks after he abruptly resigned following reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman who U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese asset.

Nvidia’s board said in a statement that it had voted unanimously in favor of his return after “a series of discussions and meeting with Mr. Huang.” The board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”

The vote came after President Trump called for Mr. Huang’s return in a social media post on Sunday night, and he immediately praised the board’s decision on Monday. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security,” he wrote.

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s chairman, said in the statement that the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.” He added, “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company.”

The return of Mr. Huang is a dramatic about-face for Nvidia, which last week said that the board had unanimously accepted his resignation. Speaking to Wall Street analysts last Tuesday, Mr. Jones — who will remain as board chair — said that the board did not plan to reinstate Mr. Huang.

Mr. Huang said in a statement that he was “honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.” He thanked the board and added that he “can’t wait to get back to work.”

The early morning news release landed just before the stock market opened, and Nvidia’s share price soared at the opening bell. The company’s stock was up more than 30 percent in early trading on Monday.

Mr. Trump, who tracks the stock market closely, wrote a social media post heralding the board’s decision. “The country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy,” he said.

It’s unlikely that Mr. Huang could have orchestrated a return without the president’s support. The men had become close allies over the past two years, working together to limit A.I. regulations and encourage the A.I. boom that has been driving the economy.

“This is less about Jensen and more about the administration,” said Patrick Moorhead, the founder of Moor Insights & Strategy, a technology analysis firm. “The speed may have been motivated by the absolute destruction of Wall Street and the tech trade. People had some time to think: What does Jensen’s absence mean to U.S. competitiveness and A. I.?”

Here’s what we’re covering:

Market reaction: Stocks were up broadly on Monday. In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12, tech stocks had dragged down the overall market. Nvidia, which has been the world’s most valuable company for much of the past two years, led the way, losing as much as $1.5 trillion of its market value. Read more ›

Driving the boom: Mr. Huang’s return is sure to boost Nvidia’s value and perhaps restore confidence in the A.I. boom. He has been the maestro of artificial intelligence, describing where the tech industry is headed. Nvidia’s chips, which have a 90 percent share of the A.I. chip market, are essential to building and running A.I. systems.

item.title: Marcia Ann Gillespie Has Died. She Led Two Pioneering Women’s Magazines
item.description:
Marcia Ann Gillespie, an editor who was a guiding force in shaping Essence as a dynamic publication for Black women in the 1970s and who later became the first Black editor in chief of the feminist publication Ms., died on Oct. 30 at her home in Manhattan. She was 82.

Her niece, Kim Mitchell, said the cause was respiratory disease.

After four years as a researcher on Black history at Time-Life Books, Ms. Gillespie was hired as second-in-command at Essence in 1970, the magazine’s first year in circulation. The magazine struggled with staff turnover and low circulation, and Ms. Gillespie, who was quick to diagnose how the magazine could be improved, was promoted to the top editing role at 26.

During the next nine years as editor in chief, she was widely credited with helping give Essence a clearer identity and mission and boost its circulation to more than 750,000.

For a core audience she identified as middle class and striving to do better, she kept the outward look of a traditional glossy — focused on beauty articles and fashion spreads — but featured content that had the capacity to surprise, like articles about how to win job promotions and coping with loneliness. She steered coverage to reflect an era when Black women were holding more political offices and rising to prominence in the wider culture.

“I want to see Essence become a force in motivating women to register and vote,” she told The Richmond Times-Dispatch in 1976, adding that she described herself as a “pragmatic feminist.”

She wrote a monthly column about Black history and pride called “Gettin’ Down,” and ran service articles about financial management. Essence also had profiles of successful Black women like the singer Aretha Franklin and accomplished actors like Louis Gossett Jr.; poetry and prose by writers like Maya Angelou and Nikki Giovanni; and thought-provoking pieces, including critiques of how Black people were portrayed on television and stories about sexual abuse of women prisoners.

Samir Husni, a scholar of magazine history, said in an interview that Essence distinguished itself from other popular Black magazines like Ebony and Jet, which tended to focus on music, entertainment and celebrities.

Essence offered “content that addressed the reality of the needs, not the wants, just the needs of the African American woman,” Mr. Husni said. “If you look at Black magazines of that era, that was something uniquely different.” Essence, he added, “made the African American woman somebody even if she was not a celebrity.”

In the wake of the Black is Beautiful movement, many of Essence’s covers featured women of all shades, hair textures and sizes — symbolizing the breadth of Black beauty and womanhood, said Susan L. Taylor, who worked as an editor under Ms. Gillespie and was editor in chief from 1981 to 2000. “She had the courage to challenge convention,” Ms. Taylor said.

Edward Lewis, one of the magazine’s founders, told The Times in 1990 that Ms. Gillespie was pivotal in redefining a magazine initially intended as a fashion-oriented publication into a more broadly appealing lifestyle and service monthly.

“She recognized that Black women could get fashion from other magazines," Mr. Lewis said. “But to really serve them well, and to strengthen our position in the marketplace, we had to give our readers what they would not find elsewhere.”

In 1979, at age 35, Ms. Gillespie made Time magazine’s “50 Faces for America’s Future” list of young leaders. She told Time that one of her biggest victories at Essence was persuading advertisers to hire Black models for ads aimed at Black consumers. “I wanted to show what Black women really are: beautiful, courageous and incredibly vital people,” she said.

After raising Essence’s profile and profitability, Ms. Gillespie stepped down from the editing role in 1980. For the next several years, she taught a publishing seminar at the University of the West Indies in Jamaica and wrote for Ms. magazine before being named executive editor in 1988.

Anne Summers, Ms.’s editor in chief, said in a statement at the time that Ms. Gillespie’s mandate was to “provide a vital link to that 20 percent of Ms. readers who are Black.”

Amid ownership changes, Ms. Gillespie took a hiatus two years later, then returned in 1992 as executive editor. The following year, she became editor in chief. “It had never crossed my mind as a possibility,” she later told Newsday. “It was clear — because of the way this industry functions — that the chances of my becoming editor in chief, except at a Black magazine, were slim to none.”

She was tasked with trying to boost the appeal of a magazine that seemed to be on a downward trajectory, with subscription and newsstand sales hovering around 200,000, or less than half of its peak in the years after its founding in the early 1970s.

Ms. Gillespie tried to improve the graphic design and lighten the tone of the articles to appeal to a younger generation of women readers.

“My major thrust is to counter the backlash against feminism,” she told Essence. “There’s this way that feminists have been characterized in the public’s mind as anti-male, anti-family, not having a whole lot of fun-and that, of course, is the last thing I ever think about.”

“Feminism in its purest sense,” she added, “means you believe in a world where women truly matter. You believe in a world where we have equality that is social and economic and political. I’m talking about a world where there is real justice.”

Mr. Husni said Ms. had struggled from the beginning, under the co-founder Gloria Steinem and then under Ms. Gillespie, who stepped down in 2001. “They tried every trick in the book,” he added, but ultimately, “it became the candle that lit all the other candles, and then faded away as the concept. I mean, what was a unique concept in the ‘70s was no longer a unique concept in the ’90s.”

Marcia Ann Gillespie, the younger of two daughters, was born on July 10, 1944, in Rockville Centre, a town on Long Island, N.Y. Her father, Charles Gillespie, ran a floor-waxing business and was a caretaker for a local Presbyterian church. Her mother, Ethel (Young) Gillespie, was a domestic worker who later managed her own catering business.

On scholarship, Ms. Gillespie graduated in 1966 from Lake Forest College, north of Chicago, with a bachelor’s degree in American studies. She then was hired at Time-Life Books, where she said she felt distinctly in the minority as a Black woman.

“I enjoyed it very much, but I also knew I wanted power,” she told the Newspaper Enterprise Association in 1976. “I worked as an editor on a Black history book for Time-Life Books. Now, if they gave me credit on the masthead, it would have become fact.”

Instead, she said she was credited for “pictures.”

“I knew I had to leave after I asked the editor in chief, ‘Did I take those pictures or pose for them?’” she recalled.

She then joined Essence.

She is survived by a sister, Charlene Gillespie.

Ms. Gillespie co-wrote “Maya Angelou: A Glorious Celebration” (2008), an illustrated biography of the writer and activist.

“I’m always very hopeful when I’m in the company of Black women,” Ms. Gillespie said in a 1976 public-television interview. “I am still, and I hope will die that way — knocked out from the kind of life force that I feel coming from Black women.”

item.title: Elon Musk Faces an A.I. Dilemma at SpaceX
item.description:
Anthropic is one of Elon Musk’s biggest competitors in artificial intelligence. It is also one of his biggest customers.

Since May, Mr. Musk’s SpaceX has made billions of dollars a month leasing computing power from its data centers to companies like Anthropic and Google. At the same time, SpaceX is developing its own A.I. products, like its chatbot Grok and A.I. agent Grok Bot.

Mr. Musk has told employees that SpaceX is falling behind in A.I. development, making it more lucrative to rent the company’s computing power out to rivals than use it to improve its own products, according to three people with knowledge of his comments.

But Mr. Musk is frustrated by the situation, the people said. In a group chat with hundreds of engineers at SpaceX’s A.I. unit, he shared data showing the company lagged competitors. And once a week, he has asked some group members to list their work in the chat to justify the use of specialized computer chips, or graphics processing units, which train A.I. systems, the people said.

In August, Mr. Musk temporarily changed the group chat name to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” according to communications viewed by The New York Times. He added a warning to employees who were not using the company’s computing resources wisely: “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.”

The tension highlights a central conflict in Mr. Musk’s A.I. push. He started an A.I. company, xAI, a year after OpenAI’s blockbuster release of ChatGPT in 2022, and has spent billions building data centers to catch up. Now, with SpaceX newly public and under pressure to show investors it can turn a profit, Mr. Musk is stuck renting much of that firepower out to the same companies he’s chasing.

That has set off a monthslong scramble for resources that has pitted the company’s ambitions — and at times even Mr. Musk’s pet projects — against its balance sheet.

The unit, renamed SpaceXSI, now generates more than half of all revenue for SpaceX, which once relied on money from government contracts to send rockets to space. SpaceX highlighted the risks of selling computing power to competitors in a prospectus before going public in June, saying the company’s data center leasing business could “create operational complexity.”

Anthropic and Google have each forged deals to lease computing power from SpaceX, with Anthropic’s valued at about $3.1 billion a month and Google’s $800 million a month. These deals could run through 2029, but could also be terminated by either party with 90 days’ notice.

Over the past few months, Anthropic has become SpaceXSI’s largest customer. Anthropic, which went public last week, has so much demand for computing power that by October, SpaceXSI needed to finish new data centers to fulfill the A.I. company’s orders, according to two people with knowledge of the work, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not permitted to speak publicly on the company’s behalf.

Representatives for SpaceX and Mr. Musk did not respond to a request for comment. Anthropic referred The Times to a portion of the company’s prospectus for its initial public offering that detailed its agreement with SpaceX.

While SpaceX has lagged rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic, Mr. Musk found an advantage in building data centers quickly. The more computing power a company has, the more powerful it can make its A.I. systems.

In 2024, Mr. Musk’s A.I. company built a data center in Memphis, one of the largest in the industry, in just 122 days. Since then, Mr. Musk has said the company has added more than one million of the specialized A.I. chips to power the technology. This month, SpaceX announced plans to invest $74 billion in data centers in Arizona and Texas.

“SpaceX makes way more money right now renting out compute than from Grok,” said Nicolas Owens, an analyst who covers SpaceX for Morningstar Research. “Grok is not the premier model in town, so I think it’s more doubtful that they would be able to tip the scale to where serving up A.I. off of their own servers is more lucrative than branching it out to Anthropic.”

Last year, xAI used less than half of the capacity of its first data center, Colossus, according to one person familiar with the project and internal documentation viewed by The Times.

While several xAI executives encouraged Mr. Musk at the time to rent out computing power to help recoup costs, he was adamant he would not do so, two people with knowledge of the conversations said.

Mr. Musk changed his mind by April, when he told xAI engineers that Anthropic had approached the company about leasing computing power, according to two people who attended the meeting. Shortly after, the company announced the deals with Anthropic and Google.

After SpaceX went public, the pressure ramped up in the company’s A.I. unit. Mr. Musk has used weekly meetings to press engineers to justify how much computing power they use, two people familiar with the conversations said. He has also become more focused on finding ways to charge those who use its A.I. products like Grok, the people said.

“At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks,” Mr. Musk wrote in August in the group chat with engineers that was viewed by The Times. “If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company. Move the needle on revenue.”

As it builds out data centers for rivals, SpaceX has quietly trimmed back its own A.I. ambitions.

In September, the company shut down a pet project of Mr. Musk’s, A.I. companions. The animated avatars could do real-time voice chats and included Ani, who would undress on command.

This fall, the company shifted resources away from another one of Mr. Musk’s top initiatives. SpaceX’s A.I. unit had been working with Tesla on a project to teach Grok how to work as an A.I. white-collar worker, called Digital Optimus.

A first step in the project was teaching the A.I. system how to play video games like Diablo and League of Legends autonomously, according to three people with knowledge of the project. After the team failed to meet Mr. Musk’s expectations, Tesla engineers were moved off the project this fall to work on the main Grok A.I. model, including its coding capabilities, two of the people said. Despite this, Mr. Musk wrote on X on Friday that the product could now reach a higher level in Diablo.

This month, Mike Nicolls, the president of the A.I. unit, announced the disbanding of the 60-member team behind Grok Imagine, an image and video-generation tool that was once a top priority, according to four people with knowledge of the cuts. Already the team’s share of computing power had shrunk, according to three people with knowledge of the project.

The cuts would “better align our structure and resources with critical business priorities,” according to an internal memo from Mr. Nicolls viewed by The Times. The Information, a tech news site, earlier reported that some members of the Grok Imagine team had been laid off.

At an employee meeting this month, Mr. Nicolls, who has overseen SpaceX’s successful satellite internet service, Starlink, repeatedly emphasized that SpaceXSI was falling behind Anthropic, said two people who attended the meeting.

Still, Mr. Musk praised SpaceX’s relationship with Anthropic last Wednesday.

“When I’ve talked to Anthropic, they tell me it is extremely likely that they will continue to rent compute from SpaceX,” he said at The Times’s DealBook conference. “And in fact that they want significantly more.”

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows the Lengths Trump Will Go to Keep A.I. Booming
item.description:
For President Trump, the stock market has long been a favored barometer for his economic agenda, one that he frequently promotes to showcase how artificial intelligence is booming on his watch.

So when scandal began to consume the chip-making giant Nvidia — toppling its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and sending financial markets into a tailspin — Mr. Trump quickly intervened. He rose to Mr. Huang’s defense and leveraged the muscle of the Oval Office to push for the embattled leader’s reinstatement.

Mr. Trump succeeded. He helped to secure Mr. Huang’s return by Monday, sending Nvidia’s stock price soaring while putting an end to a days-long market rout. In the process, the president demonstrated the lengths he was willing to go — and the risks he was ready to take — to keep both A.I. and a dependent stock market humming.

As Mr. Trump would later explain on social media, Nvidia needed Mr. Huang, and the United States needed Nvidia, to “ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The missteps of an embattled executive appeared to matter less to Mr. Trump than the economic losses that he saw on the horizon if Nvidia remained in peril.

Nvidia has a unique role in the A.I. ecosystem. It is both a pre-eminent chipmaker and a key financier for technological development, using its deep pockets and powerful semiconductors to backstop a wave of coming A.I. investment.

So the return of Mr. Huang seemed to renew a sense of exuberance on Wall Street, which may have carried a direct benefit for the president, who has previously reported holding millions of dollars in Nvidia investments. Still, Mr. Trump’s advocacy for Mr. Huang nonetheless reignited fears about his growth-at-all-costs mentality, and the extent to which his actions reflect an economy that hinges too much on the performance of a single industry.

“There is real concern about how much everyone is resting on Nvidia,” said Nidhi Hegde, the executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project, a left-leaning group. The company had become “too big to fail” in the eyes of the administration, she said.

Even Mr. Trump appeared to acknowledge the extent to which the markets had factored into his vigorous and unorthodox defense of Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia earlier this month after allegations surfaced of multiple affairs, including one with a woman who U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Asked if the stock market influenced his decision, Mr. Trump told CNBC: “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term.”

For Mr. Trump, the extraordinary lobbying campaign on behalf of Mr. Huang underscored the extent to which he has staked the economy on A.I. Even as many Americans are uneasy about the technology, Mr. Trump remains one of its fiercest defenders, and he has consistently portrayed the race to develop the technology as an existential struggle between superpowers for economic and military supremacy.

As a result, the president has largely adopted a hands-off approach to A.I., as staggering sums pour into its development. Investors and major technology giants could plow as much as $10.3 trillion into A.I. between 2025 and 2032, some estimates show, helping to buoy a U.S. economy that is tempered by high prices, sluggish hiring and geopolitical discord.

Among the big spenders is Nvidia, whose efforts have earned praise from Mr. Trump. The president has cheered on Nvidia’s stock price, and helped secure Mr. Huang a frequent spot at the White House and on Capitol Hill.

When Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia earlier this month, Mr. Trump praised his leadership and recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple executive, take over the embattled chipmaker. As markets soured over the turnover in Nvidia’s ranks — eventually dragging down major indexes with it — the president then ratcheted up his calls on the company to reinstate its old chief.

“It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.,” the president said at one point on social media.

It fit a pattern for Mr. Trump, who has staged some of his most aggressive policy interventions in response to moments of unrest in financial markets. That included revising his punishing global tariffs, as investors grew spooked over a damaging, endless trade war, and claiming progress in talks with Iran whenever the war pummeled Wall Street.

But Mr. Trump’s successful lobbying on behalf of Mr. Huang proved especially troublesome for lawmakers, including some Republicans. While the president declared that “the U.S. government does not possess any evidence that he engaged in any unlawful conduct,” some members of Congress still cited national security risks in Mr. Huang’s return. Skeptics of A.I. also saw the move as a sign that the White House had become too cozy with the tech industry.

“This looks like a decision to protect the wallets of Wall Street fat cats while putting profits ahead of our national security,” added Amy Kremer, a former leader of the Tea Party movement who is now chairwoman of Humans First, which has called for limits on data center development, in a statement.

Some economists also saw signs of a troubling dependency that would warp markets, as investors came to see Nvidia as a business that had won the favor of the president. The concerns echoed the complaints that greeted efforts by the Trump administration to take ownership stakes in private companies, including Intel.

“We want capital flowing to companies for commercial reasons,” said Scott Lincicome, the vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, a libertarian-leaning think tank. He said that investment should not follow “because they have the government’s backing or a politician’s backing, who might be making decisions not based on the commercial interests or even the national interest, but political ones.”

Mr. Trump’s intervention also arrived at a moment when policymakers across Washington were beginning to grapple openly with the extent to which the U.S. economy had become overly reliant on A.I. investment.

The concern was evident at the last meeting of the Federal Reserve. Nearly every one of the 19 officials there in October mentioned the potential fallout if A.I. investments ended up disappointing investors, who have poured billions of dollars into funding the build out, according to recently released minutes of the gathering.

Policymakers homed in on the risks stemming from the “complex and opaque financing structures” that A.I. companies are increasingly relying upon to fuel their growth, the October record showed. Raising the stakes, the Fed’s latest financial stability report, which was released earlier this month, overwhelmingly cited A.I. as the biggest threat in the eyes of market participants the central bank surveyed.

Those concerns predate the tumult facing Nvidia, reflecting investors’ continued uncertainty that they will be able to monetize their eye-popping investments into A.I. infrastructure. Against that backdrop, Shivaram Rajgopal, an accounting professor at the Columbia Business School, described Nvidia as “almost like a state-influenced enterprise,” one in which the government under Mr. Trump had established itself as a large stakeholder.

“The perception is that it’s too big to fail, and Jensen Huang is too important to fire,” he said.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows How Nvidia’s Board Was Neutered
item.description:
Six days ago, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia, said the chip maker’s 10-member board “does not intend to reinstate” Jensen Huang, who had resigned as chief executive after revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and another with a subordinate.

The board’s decision to accept Mr. Huang’s resignation was unanimous, Mr. Jones said.

But on Monday, Nvidia said that the board had “voted unanimously” to do the opposite. It was now bringing Mr. Huang back as the company’s leader. “We have every confidence in Jensen,” Mr. Jones said in a statement.

President Trump had pushed Nvidia’s board for Mr. Huang’s return, The New York Times and others reported. Mr. Trump had provided the board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges for his links with the suspected Chinese intelligence asset, who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Mr. Huang’s comeback — a rare reversal in corporate America over less than a week — immediately created whiplash and put a spotlight on Nvidia’s board and its decision-making. Corporate boards have a fiduciary duty to represent shareholders and guide companies to engage in best practices. But Mr. Trump effectively overrode Nvidia’s board in a campaign to reinstate Mr. Huang, exposing its weaknesses, corporate governance experts said.

“It neuters the board,” said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School and a former board member of Intel. “It makes the board look like lackeys of the president and therefore raises obvious questions of whether they really are good stewards of both the shareholders and the broader community.”

Nvidia declined to comment.

Nvidia’s board is facing particular criticism because Mr. Huang had violated the company’s code of conduct with his affairs with a subordinate and a customer, which the board now appeared to be disregarding, experts said.

Nvidia had also launched an internal investigation into Mr. Huang’s behavior and his ties with Alice Huang, a tech executive who U.S. intelligence had determined was a Chinese intelligence asset; the investigation has not concluded.

By reinstating Mr. Huang before finishing its investigation, Nvidia’s board could expose the company to shareholder lawsuits and political scrutiny over national security, said Eric Talley, a professor of corporate governance at Columbia Law School.

“They are essentially deciding they’re going to roll the dice on this and really, really hope that it doesn’t come up snake eyes,” Mr. Talley said.

In its statement on Monday, Nvidia’s board said its investigation would “proceed to conclusion,” and that “Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.” The board also said the company would hire a chief compliance officer who would report to its nominating and corporate governance committee.

Earlier this month, the board also formed a committee to oversee Nvidia’s national security policies, compliance with U.S. trade restrictions and risk management for global trade.

Nvidia’s board had a track record of loyalty and deference to Mr. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and built it into one of the world’s most valuable firms. Two members, Mark A. Stevens and Tench Coxe, have been on the board since 1993 after their venture capital firms invested in Nvidia. They are also among the company’s largest individual shareholders and have reaped substantial returns from their Nvidia stock.

Nvidia’s eight other board members include two former executives at a chip designer that worked with the company in the 1990s; the former chief executive of the law firm Cooley LLP, the former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs; the former chief information officer at the drugmaker Eli Lilly; the former chief marketing officer of the National Football League, the former president of Taco Bell and an engineering professor.

Before he resigned, Mr. Huang had viewed Nvidia’s board primarily as a governance requirement, rather than as an important part of the company’s strategy or execution, The Times previously reported.

Mr. Huang had flouted traditional management practices at Nvidia. He applied a flat organizational structure and had an executive staff of more than 60 people who reported to him, placing him at the center of day-to-day operations. He anointed his daughter, Madison Huang, his de facto chief of staff; and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, a leading dealmaker for the company. And Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Mr. Huang, 63.

“They gave so much of their control to him to dictate the structure of the company,” David Astorino, a senior partner at RHR International, a leadership consulting firm, said of Nvidia’s board.

After Mr. Huang resigned, his allies in Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington rallied behind him as Nvidia’s market valuation plunged by more than $1.5 trillion. The company’s share price leaped more than 30 percent on Monday after the announcement of Mr. Huang’s return.

Corporate boards have a fiduciary duty to shareholders but are “supposed to create a long-term value, not a short-term pop,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management.

In a statement on Monday, Mr. Huang said that he was honored to be back at Nvidia and expressed his gratitude to the board.

“I want to thank the Nvidia board for its confidence and deliberation through this process,” he said.

item.title: At Her 93-Year-Old Shop, She Teaches Women How to Care for Their Cars
item.description:
At the beginning of the Covid pandemic when business slowed to a near-halt, Audra Fordin was faced with a choice: She could shutter the doors of Great Bear Auto Repair and Auto Body Repair Shop in Flushing, Queens, and lay off her staff of five. Or she could take out a loan and keep her team intact through the crisis. She chose the latter.

“I earned a team that way; they knew that I was with them,” she said.

That difficult situation was one of the many that Ms. Fordin, 55, has had to navigate to keep her shop open since she took over the business from her father in 1997. Started by her great-grandfather in 1933, it’s now been in operation for 93 years.

“There’s very few businesses that make it this long, especially in an industry that’s been gobbled up by the big corporates,” she said.

That industry is also one that’s overwhelmingly male: according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, women made up only 10 percent of the automotive repair industry in 2025.

“We’re missing from the conversation,” she said.

In 2010 she started Women Auto Know, an automotive education network that hosts workshops and pop-ups focused on car maintenance and safe driving techniques to change that.

The idea was born during the 2008 recession, when a woman made an emergency stop at Great Bear because smoke had started pouring out of her car. When Ms. Fordin asked where the driver usually went for repairs, she pulled out receipts from four different mechanics.

“I was like, ‘Wow, you have no car doctor.’ How do you know if somebody gave you the wrong prescription? How do you know if somebody did something wrong?”

Working with that customer helped Ms. Fordin recognize an undeniable need to make automobile education more accessible — accidents, she said, can often occur because of poor vehicle maintenance. Since starting Women Auto Know, she has expanded its customer base, establishing Drivers Auto Know in 2022.

“It started as a business idea to save my auto shop,” she said. “It turned into my life’s work.”

She has also appeared regularly as a resident technician on MotorWeek, television’s longest running automotive series, which airs on PBS.

Ms. Fordin talked about Women Auto Know and the impact she aims to make on the automotive repair industry. These responses have been lightly edited for length and clarity.

What is it like being a woman in a male-dominated field?

I went to trade school. I was the only girl in my class, and when I went for my certifications, I was the only girl doing testing.

It used to be a lot more challenging. People would look at me and say, “Can I speak to a man?” to my face. They would call on the phone and wouldn’t want to even talk to me. But having my experience really put me in a position to not feel intimidated.

When you started Women Auto Know, how did you approach automotive education?

I realized that people, when they came to the auto shop, everybody’s always defensive and angry. So as a mechanic, I think that we’re always kind of on the defense. I realized that people weren’t actually angry, they were scared because they didn’t have information.

That changed the way that I communicated about the car. I started to use analogies relating the car to the body, like food, sex and money, and that transformed into what I call the eight essentials, where we broke up the car into these eight essential systems, and broke it down into things that everybody understands.

So it’s taking this really scary, mysterious machine and turning it into something that you can relate to.

When you started Women Auto Know business had stalled. How is it now?

We’re transforming women’s lives, and then it transforms my business. My business is no longer slow. And I’ve increased revenue threefold.

What would you say to a mechanic who might assume that teaching people how to fix their cars will make them lose customers?

Educate people, empower people, and you’ll bring in customers and you’ll earn business.

I’m not teaching them how to be a mechanic, per se. What we’re teaching them is how to talk to a mechanic, how to be proactive, how to take care of your car, how to know what to look for. How to do the maintenance so that your car will last a long time.
